etymologies.etymologyHTML: From craze (“to crush”) +‎ -y, akin to being "crazed up". Compare cracked up (“suffered a mental breakdown; be insane”).

definitions.definition: Of unsound mind; insane; demented. [from 17th c.]

quote.text: Those words appearing to be merely the ravings of superannuation, they were not regarded; but when no other traces of Mary could be found, old Andrew went up to consult this crazy dame once more, but he was not able to bring any such thing to her recollection.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter V, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Of all the queer collections of humans outside of a crazy asylum, it seemed to me this sanitarium was the cup winner.  […]  When you're well enough off so's you don't have to fret about anything but your heft or your diseases you begin to get queer, I suppose.

quote.text: Grab-a-cop-gun kinda crazy / She's poison but tasty / Yeah, people say "Run, don't walk, away"

quote.text: The girls were crazy to be introduced to him.

quote.text: We'd like to think such a kooky idea has no shot at getting on the ballot, like the previous attempts by the two main Calexiters — Marcus Ruiz Evans and Louis J. Marinelli — to get some sort of secession proposal on the ballot. But crazier things have happened.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Flawed or damaged; unsound, liable to break apart; ramshackle. [16th–19th c.]

quote.citation: 1789, John Moore, Zeluco, Valancourt, published 2008, page 203:
quote.text: Buchanan shewed her into a room adjoining to Mr. Steele's dressing-room, and separated from it by a very crazy partition.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter III, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: Piles of mean and crazy houses.

quote.citation: 1816, Francis Jeffrey, “Memoirs of Madame de Larochejaquelein”, in The Edinburgh Review February 1816:
quote.text: They  […]  got a crazy boat to carry them to the island.

quote.citation: 1859, Charles Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities:
quote.text: Casement windows opened, crazy doors were unbarred, and people came forth shivering—chilled, as yet, by the new sweet air.

quote.citation: 1710 March 28 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison; Richard Steele et al.], “FRIDAY, March 17, 1709–1710”, in The Spectator, number 15; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume I, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: One of great riches, but a crazy constitution.The spelling has been modernized.

quote.citation: c. 1793, Edward Gibbon, Memoirs, Penguin, published 1990, page 61:
quote.text: My poor aunt has often told me  […]  how long she herself was apprehensive lest my crazy frame, which is now of common shape, should remain for ever crooked and deformed.

quote.citation: 2002, Gina Riley, Jane Turner, That's Unusual: Scripts from Kath and Kim, Series 2, page 67:
quote.text: I'm flat out. It's crazy stupid here, Kim.

definitions.definition: (slang, countable) An insane or eccentric person; a crackpot.

quote.text: Allen Gregory DeLongpre: Now drink up, you knuckleheads! Have a blast! It's our night, you crazies! Chloe, where are you?
Then again, her whole evening was full of crazy, and she didn't know what else to do.
